planting.note: Soak seed 24 hours before sowing to break the corky bract and improve uptake; sow in late summer, autumn, or early spring in well-drained, alkaline soil, avoiding the hottest and coldest months, and establish seedlings before the first dry season.

directions: A large, densely branched silver-grey shrub traditionally harvested by Aboriginal communities for its salty, mineral-rich leaves and seed bracts. Pick young leaves to eat raw or lightly cooked as a salt-forward green, or dry and grind the seed bracts into a seasoning flour. Thrives on neglect in hot, saline, low-rainfall sites and doubles as a windbreak or informal hedge; avoid overwatering, which encourages lanky growth and reduces flavor concentration.

planting.note: Plant rooted divisions or nursery liners in spring into consistently moist, boggy soil in part shade to full sun; spreads by runners, so site it where it can be contained or allowed to naturalize along a damp bed edge.

directions: An aromatic, peppermint-scented Australian native herb long used by Aboriginal people for tea, flavoring, and as an insect repellent. The soft foliage spreads readily by runners in consistently damp ground, making it useful as a moisture-loving herb-garden groundcover near ponds or low spots. Harvest leaves and stem tips through summer for fresh or dried mint flavoring; cut back hard after flowering to keep growth compact and leafy.

planting.note: Transplant container-grown stock in spring into humus-rich, well-drained soil in part to full shade, especially while young; this rainforest understory shrub resents hot sun and dry wind.

directions: A multi-trunked rainforest shrub whose coppery, laurel-like leaves give one of its common names, grown for its urn-shaped, cream-colored flowers followed by sweet, creamy-pulped fruit. Known traditionally as bolwarra and eaten fresh or cooked into jam, the fruit resembles a small, custardy guava and is best picked when fully soft. Give it a sheltered, shaded spot with reliable moisture, since both foliage and fruit quality suffer in direct sun or drought.

planting.note: Start seed under cover in spring and transplant out once established, or set out nursery divisions; prefers sandy, well-drained soil with a salty tang and tolerates coastal exposure, light shade, and brackish splash.

directions: A low, sprawling coastal herb traditionally gathered by Aboriginal people along dunes and tidal margins and used fresh or cooked much like parsley or celery. The tender, salty-flavored leaves and stems pair naturally with seafood, soups, and stews, while the seed can be crushed as a seasoning. Grow it in sandy, free-draining soil with some protection from the hottest sun, and harvest leaves regularly to keep the sprawling rosettes producing tender new growth.

planting.note: Direct sow after soil has warmed and frost danger has passed; this fast, high-yielding Indonesian variety was bred for lowland tropical and subtropical conditions and performs best with warm soil and a long, humid growing season.

directions: A high-yielding Indonesian soybean variety developed by the national legume research program and widely favored by tempeh producers for its large, pale-yellow seeds and short growing season. Grobogan matures faster than most tempeh soybeans, reaching harvest in under three months with notably large hundred-seed weight compared to older local varieties. Grown extensively across Java as a replacement for imported soybeans in traditional tempeh and tahu production.

planting.note: Direct sow once soil is reliably warm after frost danger passes; bred for Indonesian lowland cropping, it wants a long warm season and even moisture through pod fill.

directions: A widely grown Indonesian soybean variety prized by artisanal tempeh makers for producing a more savory-tasting, brighter, and longer-lasting tempeh than imported soybean varieties. It has a somewhat longer season than Grobogan but is valued for consistent yellow seed color and good disease tolerance under humid field conditions. Released through Indonesia's national legume breeding program, it remains one of the most popular domestic alternatives to imported soybeans for traditional soy foods.

planting.note: Direct sow in warm soil after frost danger passes; a compact, lodging-resistant older Indonesian variety that still performs reliably in humid lowland conditions.

directions: Released in Indonesia in the mid-1980s from a cross involving an older introduction line, Wilis became one of the country's most widely grown older soybean varieties thanks to its compact, lodging-resistant habit and tolerance of rust and virus pressure. Plants stay short and determinate with purple flowers and small, oval yellow seeds, making it an easy variety to grow in home plots. Though newer varieties like Grobogan and Anjasmoro have largely overtaken it commercially, Wilis remains a reliable, well-documented heritage choice for tempeh and tofu production.
sources: Badan Litbang Pertanian (Indonesian Agency for Agricultural Research and Development)
